newsitem.title: UK: Millennium bug to lead to huge claims - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Millennium bug to lead to huge claims - lawyer.

text.p: Claims arising from the millennium computer bug will lead to litigation costing around $1 trillion in the United States alone, underwriters at Lloyd's of London were told on Thursday.

"We forecast $1 trillion dollars of litigation in the U.S.. And when you consider that the total for litigation for all other liabilities including asbestos, tort and pollution is $300 billion, you see the millennium issue is much more serious," Jeff Jinnett of U.S. law firm LeBoeuf, Lamb, Greene & MacRae told a conference organised by Lloyd's.

The millennium bug stems from computer programming in the sixties which sought to save memory by using only the last two numbers of a year when recording the date. When the year 2000 comes, computers could read the date as being in the year 1900, bringing havoc to thousands of business operations.
Jinnett said those who make losses as a result will seek compensation through the courts.

Shareholders will sue companies for poor management, information technology consultants will be sued for malpractice and computer suppliers will face product liability actions for selling non-compliant products, Jinnett said.
"Directors and officers policies and professional liability policies will probably have to cover these claims," Jinnett told the insurers.

The comments were made at the first Lloyd's professional indemnity conference -- organised by Lloyd's to boost its image after recovering from 8.1 billion stg ($13.3 billion) losses between 1988 and 1992 -- during a session entitled "The year 2000 - myth or reality".
"If anyone here thinks this is a myth, the reality will be disaster," said Robin Guenier, executive director of Taskforce 2000.
He estimated it would cost 31 billion stg to fix the problem in Britain alone.
"But there are not enough resources to fix it. In the UK it would take the commitment of the entire IT (information technology) industry, and that is not about to happen," Guenier said.
He added that companies which have not started work on the problem do not have enough time to fix it, as system changes will have to be done by the end of 1998 to allow time for testing.
"Business leaders and computer specialists are doing too little. It is not a matter that can be delegated to the IT department. It needs the concentration of people at the very top," he said.
-- Reuters Insurance News +44 171 542 2770 ($ = 0.609 British Pounds Sterling)
